evaluation.positioning_hook: A church custodian trapped in a controlling marriage finally chooses his daughter over the woman who monitors every move, and the escape becomes a custody fight.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is immediate and legible: a man and his daughter trying to get out of an abusive home. That gives the script a clear audience in adult drama and issue-driven prestige lanes, though the material is more targeted than broad four-quadrant fare.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands quickly through the opening kitchen confrontation, the church refuge, and the later custody escalation. The story engine is easy to explain in one breath, with the domestic control dynamic and the public/legal fallout clearly established.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ralph and Eleanor have a clean emotional spine, and Diane is written with enough control and volatility to hold the room. The characters function well for the feature, though the supporting cast largely serves the central triangle rather than opening many additional character lanes.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar domestic-abuse framework and places it in a church/school/custody setting, which gives it some distinction. The execution stays close to the expected dramatic vocabulary, so the boldness comes more from framing than from formal surprise.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The escalation is clean: accusation, visible injury, leaving, hospital, custody hearing, final separation. The structure keeps moving, though several beats are built around repeated confrontations that reinforce the same emotional turn rather than adding new pressure each time.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core setup is instantly understandable and emotionally resonant, but it reads as a recognizable domestic drama engine rather than a newly discovered one. The church custodian angle adds texture, yet the central dramatic shape remains familiar.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The church, school, home, and courtroom give the story a grounded civic texture, and Ralph’s custodial routine is specific enough to feel lived-in. The world is primarily a container for the central conflict rather than a system with many story-generating layers.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistent and controlled, with quiet dread giving way to plainspoken release. The script knows what kind of movie it is, even if the emotional register stays in a familiar prestige-drama lane.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in Ralph’s silence, Father Sears’s concern, and Diane’s shifting control tactics. The script hints at a fuller interior life beneath the surface, though the feature stays focused on the immediate escape narrative.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Ralph-Diane-Eleanor triangle carries the film effectively, and Father Sears adds a useful pressure valve. Beyond that core, the supporting relationships are functional rather than independently generative.

notable_requirements: School hallway, locker room, office, and football cleanup areas

technical.sfx_needs: Practical glass breakage, mug throw, physical shoves, and a visible injury makeup beat.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Prestige streaming drama or limited theatrical drama
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with festival-to-platform potential; the engine is the domestic escape and custody aftermath.

cost.note: Contemporary, contained locations, no VFX, and only minor practical effects keep the budget in a modest feature range.

cast.note: The film depends on three central performances and includes a child actor, but the overall cast is compact.

location.note: The story moves through home, church, school, hospital, motel, and courtroom, with several distinct interiors and multiple night scenes.

content.note: Domestic violence, intimidation, injury, and custody conflict place it firmly in mature-drama territory.

rights.note: No named music, brands, or real-person references are present in the script.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The opening establishes the control dynamic instantly.
strengths.what_it_means: That first kitchen sequence gives a producer a clean, immediate read on the movie: this is a domestic thriller-drama with a clear emotional engine and no time wasted. It will attract buyers looking for contained, actor-driven material that can be sold on premise and performance rather than spectacle.
strengths.evidence: The 5:12 a.m. lunch-packing routine, the phone check, the line 'you belong to me,' and the kiss that lands as possession rather than affection.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ralph is a playable, quiet lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives an actor a contained, internal showcase built around restraint, endurance, and the moment a man stops absorbing harm and starts choosing himself. That is exactly the kind of part prestige drama buyers and mid-career actors chase when they want a role with emotional authority and awards-adjacent gravity.
strengths.evidence: Ralph’s silence through the early abuse, his work routine at the church and school, and the later line that he is 'not carrying it anymore.'

strengths.dimension_or_area: Diane has a strong, volatile screen presence.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives an actress a role that can move between charm, menace, and wounded control in the same scene, which is a strong packaging lever for performance-driven buyers. Actors who want a morally charged, scene-commanding part with real volatility will see the appeal immediately.
strengths.evidence: Diane’s rapid shifts from accusation to tenderness, the jersey being cut in half, and the hospital-room return where she tries to reset the relationship.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The church setting adds moral texture.
strengths.what_it_means: Placing the story inside a church and school gives the film a public-facing pressure that expands it beyond a private marriage story. That makes it attractive to buyers who want grounded drama with community stakes and to directors who like character conflict embedded in institutions.
strengths.evidence: Ralph’s work at St. Andrew’s, Father Sears noticing the bruising, and Diane confronting him in front of people at church.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The custody turn gives the ending commercial lift.
strengths.what_it_means: The move from escape story to custody battle broadens the emotional stakes and gives the feature a second act of consequence beyond simply leaving the house. That helps the script play to audiences who want catharsis plus aftermath, and it gives streamers a clean hook for adult viewers.
strengths.evidence: The lawyer’s phone call, the courtroom sequence, Eleanor’s testimony, and the supervised visitation ruling.

strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of contained contemporary drama that can be mounted without a large company, heavy effects, or expensive set pieces. That makes it appealing to indie financiers, streamer acquisition teams, and directors looking for a strong reel piece that stays inside a manageable budget band.
strengths.evidence: Home, church, school, hospital, motel, and courtroom are the main locations, with no VFX and only minor practical action.

whats_special.headline: Silent Bruises is a contained, performance-forward domestic drama with a clean commercial spine: a church custodian finally leaves a controlling marriage, only to face the custody fight that makes the escape real. The script’s strongest asset is its castable triangle — a restrained male lead, a volatile wife role, and a daughter who turns the story into a true survival narrative.

lead_characters.name: Ralph Dinozzo
lead_characters.hook: Ralph is a quiet, habit-driven man whose life has been reduced to routines, work shifts, and strategic silence. He reads as someone who has spent years making himself smaller to keep the peace, and the movie’s emotional charge comes from watching that containment finally crack into action.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom — a contained man whose stillness becomes the performance. Actors who excel at internal pressure, moral awakening, and late-blooming resolve will see a role that can carry a whole film on restraint alone.

lead_characters.name: Diane Dinozzo
lead_characters.hook: Diane is controlling, watchful, and emotionally mercurial, with a need to dominate every room she enters. What makes her specific is the way her affection and aggression live side by side; she can sound like a loving wife one beat and a jailer the next, which keeps every interaction charged.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl — a role that lets an actor weaponize charm, precision, and emotional volatility. Mid-career actresses looking for a scene-stealing part with menace, intelligence, and awards-friendly complexity will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Eleanor Dinozzo
lead_characters.hook: Eleanor is the story’s moral witness: observant, increasingly brave, and forced to grow up fast inside a house where truth is dangerous. She begins as the child watching everything and becomes the person who names what the adults have spent the film avoiding.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of breakthrough role that gave Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project or Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 their emotional authority — a young performer getting to play intelligence under pressure. Rising teen actors with dramatic instincts will want the chance to anchor the film’s turning point and carry the audience’s trust.

lead_characters.name: Father Maxwell Sears
lead_characters.hook: Father Sears is the calm outside the storm, a priest who notices more than he says and offers Ralph the first real permission to stop carrying everything alone. He functions as a moral witness and a practical ally, giving the film a humane counterweight without taking over the central conflict.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, quietly authoritative supporting part that actors like Mark Ruffalo in Spotlight or Paul Dano in 12 Years a Slave have used to create emotional gravity without overselling it. Character actors who specialize in empathy, restraint, and moral clarity will be drawn to the role’s precision.

lead_characters.name: Ralph’s Attorney
lead_characters.hook: Ralph’s attorney is a functional but important pressure-release character who helps translate the private abuse into public consequence. The role is pragmatic, composed, and built to carry courtroom clarity rather than personal backstory.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of efficient legal-support role that actors like Marcia Gay Harden in smaller prestige dramas or Jeffrey Wright in courtroom material can make feel essential through authority and precision. Working character actors who like clean, scene-specific utility will see an easy fit.

lead_characters.name: Diane’s Attorney
lead_characters.hook: Diane’s attorney is the polished public face of her control, helping her convert private chaos into a controlled legal narrative. The character is less about personality than about the institutional polish that makes Diane’s version of events sound plausible.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of sharp, procedural supporting part that actors in the Ann Dowd or Michael Stuhlbarg lane can elevate with stillness and tactical intelligence. It gives a performer the chance to play subtext inside a courtroom framework without needing a large footprint.

lead_characters.name: Judge
lead_characters.hook: The Judge is the film’s final institutional voice: measured, unsentimental, and there to turn private pain into a binding decision. The role is brief but decisive, giving the courtroom sequence its formal weight.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of concise authority role that actors like Cherry Jones or J. Smith-Cameron can make memorable in a handful of scenes. It offers a clean, high-trust courtroom presence that lands the film’s final legal turn.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a tense, actor-first domestic drama with real emotional restraint.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with at least one or two character-driven features, or TV directors moving into features who already know how to stage intimate conflict without overcutting it. The material rewards performance blocking, controlled escalation, and a clean visual language that lets silence and proximity do the work.
director_appeal.detail: The film gives a director a contained pressure cooker with three central performances and a clear emotional arc, which is ideal for someone whose reel already shows command of actors and tension. It will appeal to directors who like prestige drama, social realism, and the kind of material that can be shot efficiently while still feeling serious and cinematic.

buyer_appeal.detail: The package can be built around one strong male lead, one volatile female lead, and a young breakout role, so a buyer can attach off performances rather than effects or scale. The contained contemporary footprint and custody-drama hook fit the current streamer appetite for adult, issue-driven features that travel cleanly on title and premise.

considerations.area: The church-school-home triangle does the heavy lifting.
considerations.detail: The story’s emotional geography is strongest when Ralph’s refuge, work, and home are in constant collision. A next pass could consider whether one of the school or church beats can absorb a function from another location, which would protect the same pressure while keeping the footprint even tighter.

considerations.area: The middle repeats the same confrontation shape.
considerations.detail: Several beats in Act II return to accusation, denial, and physical escalation in a similar rhythm. One direction would be to let one of those scenes turn on a new kind of pressure — public exposure, a choice in front of Eleanor, or a tactical move from Ralph — so each escalation adds a fresh layer.

considerations.area: Father Sears can carry more narrative function.
considerations.detail: He already serves as the first person to name what Ralph is living through, which makes him a natural anchor for the outside world. There is room to clarify whether he is only a witness or also a practical bridge to help Ralph move from recognition into action, which would deepen the church thread without expanding cast.

considerations.area: The custody turn is the cleanest commercial expansion.
considerations.detail: The courtroom sequence gives the feature a second engine beyond escape, which is a strong positioning advantage for buyers and festivals alike. If the goal is maximum audience clarity, the version of the script that keeps the legal aftermath front and center will make the title easier to sell on premise.
